original_question: A proper vertex coloring is called a 2-homogeneous coloring when exactly 2 colors appear in the open neighborhood of every vertex. Are there only finitely many connected bridgeless cubic graphs that do not admit a 2-homogeneous coloring?
target_in_paper: Section 5, Problem 5.2 (Homogeneous coloring of cubic graphs).
correct_elements: Your draft already identifies the right open problem almost verbatim: it uses the correct notion of a 2-homogeneous coloring, and it keeps the exact graph class from the paper—connected bridgeless cubic graphs—together with the intended finiteness question.
missing_details: Make the coloring fully explicit as a proper vertex-coloring c: V(G) -> C.
Define the open neighborhood as N(v) = {u in V(G) : uv in E(G)} and state the condition as |c(N(v))| = 2 for every vertex v.
If complete stand-alone phrasing is desired, unpack 'cubic' as 3-regular.
If complete stand-alone phrasing is desired, unpack 'bridgeless' as having no cut-edge.
State explicitly that G is finite, which is the standard ambient convention in the paper's graph-theoretic setting.
refined_question: Let G be a finite connected bridgeless cubic graph. Are there only finitely many such graphs for which no proper vertex-coloring c: V(G) -> C satisfies |c(N(v))| = 2 for every vertex v in V(G), where N(v) denotes the open neighborhood of v?
justification: The draft is aiming at the second official open problem in Section 5. In the paragraph introducing that section, the paper defines a k-homogeneous coloring as a proper vertex coloring in which exactly k colors appear in the open neighborhood of every vertex, then specializes to the 2-homogeneous case for cubic graphs, and finally states Problem 5.2 as the finiteness question for connected bridgeless cubic graphs. I therefore kept the scope exactly there and did not drift to the neighboring Problem 5.1 about whether four colors always suffice. The only sharpening needed was to formalize the coloring and neighborhood notation so the question is fully stand-alone.
